# Two defining relations and complete atomic factorization theory for thirteen-smooth Jordan–Pólya numbers

## Finding
Let \(\mathcal J_{13}\) be the multiplicative monoid of Jordan–Pólya numbers all of whose prime divisors belong to \(\{2,3,5,7,11,13\}\), including \(1\). Its eight multiplicative atoms are precisely
\[
2!,\quad3!,\quad5!,\quad7!,\quad11!,\quad13!,\quad14!,\quad15!.
\]
**The entire equality relation among products of these atoms is generated by exactly two relations:**
\[
(14!)(5!)=(15!)(2!)^3,\qquad
(7!)(13!)=(15!)(2!)^2(3!).
\]
These relations are minimal and independent: the semigroup algebra of \(\mathcal J_{13}\), over any field, is a complete intersection of codimension two. Every set of lengths of atomic factorizations is a singleton or an uninterrupted arithmetic progression with difference \(2\). The global delta set is exactly \(\{2\}\), and the catenary degree of \(\mathcal J_{13}\) is exactly \(4\).

An exact number-of-factorizations formula and exact length-set endpoints are given below. Here *atomic* always means factorization into the displayed eight indecomposable generators, not a factorization into arbitrary factorials \(k!\); these are different counting problems.

## Assumptions and scope
A Jordan–Pólya number is a positive integer expressible as a finite product of factorials. The empty product is \(1\). Because \(17\) divides every factorial of index at least \(17\), \(\mathcal J_{13}\) is generated by the factorials of indices \(2\) through \(16\). Direct factorial identities reduce these to the eight generators in the Finding.

For any \(13\)-smooth positive integer \(N\), write \(e_p=\nu_p(N)\). Define the six integral **prime-factorial coordinates**
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_1&=e_2-e_3-2e_5-e_{13},&c_2&=e_3-e_5-e_7-e_{11}-e_{13},\\
c_3&=e_5-e_7-e_{11},&c_4&=e_7-e_{11},\\
c_5&=e_{11}-e_{13},&c_6&=e_{13}.
\end{aligned}
\]
They arise by inversion of the triangular integer valuation matrix for the six prime-index factorials, whose diagonal entries are all \(1\). Define \([z]_+=\max(0,z)\), \(r_0=\max(0,-c_3)\), \(m=\min(c_4,c_6)\), and \(C=\sum_{i=1}^6c_i\).

For \(N\in\mathcal J_{13}\), the exact number \(F(N)\) of atomic factorizations is
\[
F(N)=\sum_{t=\max(0,-c_2)}^{m}
\left[\min\!\left(t,\left\lfloor\frac{c_1+2t}{3}\right\rfloor\right)-r_0+1\right]_+.
\]
The convention is that an empty sum is zero. The membership condition \(c_5\ge0\) is automatic for \(N\in\mathcal J_{13}\); for a general \(13\)-smooth integer, set \(F(N)=0\) if \(c_5<0\), and otherwise the same sum tests membership as well.

Set
\[
t_0=\max\!\left(0,-c_2,r_0,
\left\lceil\frac{3r_0-c_1}{2}\right\rceil\right),
\quad
s_0=\max\!\left(0,\left\lceil\frac{t_0-c_1}{3}\right\rceil\right).
\]
For every \(N\in\mathcal J_{13}\), its **exact set of atomic-factorization lengths** is
\[
\mathcal L(N)=\{C+2s:s_0\le s\le m-r_0,\ s\in\mathbb Z\}.
\]
In particular all these lengths have the same parity, and all intermediate values of that parity occur.

## Proof
**1. The eight atoms and coordinate model.** The identities
\[
\begin{gathered}
4!=(2!)^2 3!,\qquad6!=3!5!,\qquad8!=(2!)^3 7!,\\
9!=2!(3!)^2 7!,\qquad10!=3!5!7!,\qquad12!=2!3!11!,\\
16!=(2!)^4 15!
\end{gathered}
\]
cover every factorial between \(2!\) and \(16!\) except the displayed eight. Each prime-index factorial \(p!\) is an atom: a factorial generator carrying the prime \(p\) has value at least \(p!\), and any nontrivial factorization of \(p!\) must include a factor carrying \(p\), forcing the factor to be \(p!\) itself. In the prime-factorial coordinate basis, \(14!\) has vector \(u=(1,-1,-1,1,0,1)\) and \(15!\) has vector \(v=(-2,-1,0,1,0,1)\). The negative coordinates exclude representations of \(14!\) by prime-index generators; \(15!\) cannot be formed by prime-index generators and \(14!\) because its first coordinate is \(-2\), whereas subtracting any nonnegative multiple of \(u\) only decreases that coordinate. Thus both are atoms.

**2. Every factorization and its unique reduced form.** For a factorization with exponents \((a_1,\ldots,a_6,r,s)\) on the eight atoms, put \(t=r+s\). The equation for its prime-factorial coordinates is exactly
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_1&=c_1+2t-3r,&a_2&=c_2+t,&a_3&=c_3+r,\\
a_4&=c_4-t,&a_5&=c_5,&a_6&=c_6-t,
\end{aligned}
\]
subject to \(r,s,a_i\ge0\). Rewrite each instance of \((14!)(5!)\) as \((15!)(2!)^3\), and each instance of \((7!)(13!)\) as \((15!)(2!)^2(3!)\). These moves preserve \(N\). In the first move \(r\) decreases by one; in the second \(r\) remains fixed while \(a_4+a_6\) decreases by two. Therefore the lexicographically ordered pair \((r,a_4+a_6)\) decreases strictly at each step. Rewriting terminates.

A factorization is irreducible under these moves precisely when \(r a_3=0\) and \(a_4a_6=0\). In an irreducible factorization \(a_3=c_3+r\ge0\) forces \(r=r_0\), and \(a_4=c_4-t\), \(a_6=c_6-t\) force \(t=m\). All remaining exponents are then fixed by the displayed equations. Consequently every factorization of \(N\) terminates at exactly the *same* reduced factorization. Two products of the eight atoms have equal integer values if and only if the two elementary moves and their inverses connect them. This is a complete presentation, not merely a list of valid identities.

**3. Minimality and complete intersection.** Six prime-index factorial valuation vectors constitute a unimodular basis for the exponent lattice \(\mathbb Z^6\); adding \(u,v\) gives an eight-generator map with relation-lattice rank \(8-6=2\). Any monoid presentation must contain at least two independent relations to span this lattice. The displayed two relations generate the entire congruence by step 2, so they are a minimal presentation. Equivalently, for indeterminates \(X_2,X_3,X_5,X_7,X_{11},X_{13},X_{14},X_{15}\), the kernel of the map sending \(X_j\) to \(j!\) in the semigroup algebra is the ideal
\[
\left(X_{14}X_5-X_{15}X_2^3,\quad X_7X_{13}-X_{15}X_2^2X_3\right).
\]
This prime toric ideal has height two in a polynomial ring in eight variables and is generated by two elements; therefore it is a complete-intersection ideal, over any field.

**4. Exact factorization count and lengths.** For a given \(t=r+s\), nonnegativity of the six \(a_i\) above is equivalent to
\[
\max(0,-c_3)\le r\le
\min\!\left(t,\left\lfloor\frac{c_1+2t}{3}\right\rfloor\right),
\quad \max(0,-c_2)\le t\le m,
\quad c_5\ge0.
\]
Counting integer \(r\) for each integer \(t\) proves the formula for \(F(N)\). Summing the eight factorization exponents gives
\(a_1+\cdots+a_6+r+s=C+2s\). The least feasible \(t\) is \(t_0\), found by choosing the smallest feasible \(r=r_0\). At that \(t\), the largest feasible \(r\) is \(\min(t_0,\lfloor(c_1+2t_0)/3\rfloor)\), so the least possible \(s=t-r\) is \(s_0\). The largest possible \(s\) is attained at \(t=m,r=r_0\), giving \(m-r_0\).

Each defining move changes the factorization length by exactly \(2\). Since step 2 connects *every* pair of factorizations, a path between one of minimum length and one of maximum length must visit every intermediate length of the same parity. This proves the claimed exact arithmetic progression, and the nontrivial relation examples show that the global delta set is \(\{2\}\).

**5. Catenary degree.** For two atomic factorizations the standard distance is the maximum number of atoms remaining on either side after canceling their componentwise gcd. Each elementary relation replaces two atoms by four atoms with disjoint supports, and has distance \(4\). Step 2 thus gives a \(4\)-chain between every two factorizations, proving the catenary degree is at most \(4\). The element \((14!)(5!)\) has exactly two atomic factorizations, namely \((14!)(5!)\) and \((15!)(2!)^3\), as follows from the feasibility formula with coordinates \((1,-1,0,1,0,1)\). Their distance is \(4\), so no \(3\)-chain connects them; the catenary degree is exactly \(4\).

## Verification
Run the standalone `python3 verify.py` with Python 3. It independently enumerates every atomic factorization of all members up to the explicit integer bound \(10^{20}\), verifies the two factorial identities, checks all eight generators are atoms, compares the independent enumeration with the closed exact factorization count, verifies normal-form uniqueness, confirms each elementary rewrite remains within the factorization set, and tests every exact length-set interval. A fresh execution gave:

`VERIFY_OK bound=100000000000000000000 distinct_numbers=9556 factorizations=10008 relation_checks=2 full_count_and_normal_form_checks=9556 atomic_generators=8 length_set_checks=9556`

These finite comparisons are corroboration, not a substitute for the infinite symbolic proof above. The script enumerates only products of the eight atoms, not arbitrary factorial representations, in accordance with the claim.

## Relationship to prior work
De Koninck, Doyon, Razafindrasoanaivolala, and Verreault investigate Jordan–Pólya counting and explicitly distinguish nonunique arbitrary-factorial representations from unique prime-factorial representations. Earlier fixed-support classifications establish a free monoid through largest prime \(11\), then a membership inequality and one canonical representation for largest prime \(13\). The latter result supplies the same prime-factorial coordinate vectors and feasibility inequalities; this is acknowledged as a substantive shared starting point. It does **not** state a presentation generating *every equality among atomic products*, nor compute the complete sets of atomic lengths, delta set, or exact catenary degree. The contribution here is the minimal complete two-relation quotient structure and its factorization-theoretic consequences, not a new membership criterion. The closed count formula explicitly refines those previously available inequalities; by itself it is not claimed as the main novelty.

## Limitations
This result concerns only Jordan–Pólya numbers with no prime divisor greater than \(13\), and their factorizations into the eight **atoms** of that monoid. It does not count representations using arbitrary factorials, nor characterize the next prime-support stratum. An unindexed earlier treatment or an unstated presentation derivable from prior coordinate work remains an originality risk. The computational check has a finite cutoff; all unbounded assertions use the exact symbolic rewriting proof.
